theory.overview: Digital signatures provide the cryptographic equivalent of handwritten signatures: proof of authenticity, non-repudiation, and message integrity in the digital realm. Combining the one-way property of hash functions with the asymmetric power of public key cryptography, digital signatures allow anyone to verify a message came from you (authenticity) while ensuring you cannot later deny sending it (non-repudiation). When you sign a document, you're essentially performing a mathematical operation that only your private key can perform—but anyone with your public key can verify. Digital signatures power software updates, secure email, cryptocurrency transactions, legal contracts, and countless trust mechanisms in our digital infrastructure.

sections.title: How Digital Signatures Work
sections.content: The signature process combines hashing and asymmetric encryption. First, hash the message to produce a fixed-size digest—this is more efficient than signing the entire message and binds the signature to the exact content. Then, encrypt that hash with your private key (in RSA: s = h^d mod n). This encrypted hash is the digital signature. Verification reverses the process: anyone can decrypt the signature using your public key to recover the hash, then independently hash the received message and compare. If they match, the message is authentic (from you) and unaltered (hasn't been tampered). The security relies on the fact that only your private key could have created a signature that decrypts correctly with your public key.
keyPoints: Sign: hash message, encrypt hash with private key
Verify: decrypt signature with public key, compare to message hash
Binding: signature is tied to both signer identity and message content
Non-repudiation: signer cannot deny creating the signature

sections.title: RSA Signatures
sections.content: RSA signatures leverage the mathematical relationship between encryption and decryption. In RSA, e and d are inverses: (m^e)^d = (m^d)^e = m mod n. This symmetry enables signing—encrypt with private key (normally used for decryption), and anyone can 'decrypt' with public key to verify. The signature process: compute message hash h = SHA-256(m), compute signature s = h^d mod n. Verification: compute h' = s^e mod n, verify h' equals SHA-256(m). For security, RSA signatures use padding schemes like PKCS#1 v1.5 or PSS (Probabilistic Signature Scheme). PSS is recommended as it provides provable security—each signature includes randomness, making signature forgery equivalent to solving the RSA problem directly.
keyPoints: RSA signing: s = h^d mod n (sign with private key)
RSA verification: h = s^e mod n (verify with public key)
Padding required: raw RSA is vulnerable to attacks

sections.title: ECDSA: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm
sections.content: ECDSA, used in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and TLS, provides equivalent security to RSA with much smaller keys—256-bit ECDSA matches 3072-bit RSA security. ECDSA operates on elliptic curves over finite fields. Key generation: select random private key d, compute public key Q = d × G where G is a generator point on the curve. Signing: select random k, compute R = k × G = (x, y), set r = x mod n, compute s = k^(-1) × (h + r × d) mod n. Signature is (r, s). Verification: compute w = s^(-1), u1 = h × w, u2 = r × w, then check if u1 × G + u2 × Q equals R. The security relies on the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem: finding d from Q = d × G is computationally infeasible.
keyPoints: Uses elliptic curve mathematics over finite fields
Smaller signatures, faster computation than RSA
Requires randomness: bad randomness leaks private key (Sony PlayStation 3 hack)

sections.title: Applications and Security
sections.content: Digital signatures enable trust across countless applications. Software distribution: OS vendors sign updates so your device verifies authenticity before installation, preventing malware injection. Code signing: developers sign applications so operating systems warn users about unverified software. Document signing: PDFs with embedded signatures provide legal non-repudiation. Blockchain: transactions are signed to prove ownership of funds without revealing private keys. Certificate authorities sign TLS certificates, creating trust chains that secure web browsing. Security considerations: private key protection is paramount—compromised signing keys enable forged signatures. Hardware security modules (HSMs) store keys in tamper-resistant hardware. Timestamping services prove when signatures were created, preventing backdating attacks. Signature algorithms evolve as cryptanalysis advances—RSA-2048 minimum, ECDSA-P256 standard, post-quantum algorithms being standardized.
keyPoints: Blockchain: prove ownership without revealing keys
Key protection: HSMs, secure enclaves essential

practiceProblems.title: Signature Properties
practiceProblems.description: What three security properties does a digital signature provide?

solution.answer: Authenticity (message from claimed sender), Integrity (message not modified), Non-repudiation (sender cannot deny)
solution.explanation: Digital signatures provide all three: only the private key holder can create valid signatures (authenticity), any message change invalidates the signature (integrity), and the signature cryptographically proves origin (non-repudiation).

practiceProblems.title: Why Hash First?
practiceProblems.description: Why do we hash the message before signing instead of signing the message directly?
hints: RSA has maximum message size limits
Large messages would be slow to sign

solution.answer: Hashing produces fixed-size input, enables signing large messages efficiently, and creates strong binding between signature and content
solution.explanation: Signing directly limits message size and is computationally expensive for large data. Hashing produces fixed-size input (256 bits) while ensuring any message change invalidates the signature through avalanche effect.

practiceProblems.title: RSA vs ECDSA Keys
practiceProblems.description: Compare key sizes: 256-bit ECDSA provides equivalent security to what size RSA key?

solution.explanation: Elliptic curve cryptography provides equivalent security with much smaller keys due to the hardness of the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem compared to integer factorization.

practiceProblems.title: Signature Forgery
practiceProblems.description: Why can't an attacker forge my signature if they know my public key?
practiceProblems.latex: Given (e, n) and m, compute s where Verify((e,n), m, s) = true
hints: Creating valid signature requires private key
Verification uses public key (available to all)
Only private key can decrypt to valid hash

solution.answer: Creating a valid signature requires the private key; knowing the public key only allows verification, not signature generation
solution.explanation: The one-way nature of trapdoor functions ensures that while anyone can verify using the public key, only the private key holder can create valid signatures. Computing s = h^d mod n without knowing d requires solving the RSA problem, which is as hard as factoring n.

practiceProblems.title: Modified Message
practiceProblems.description: Alice signs 'Pay Bob $100'. Eve intercepts and changes it to 'Pay Bob $1000'. Will the signature still verify?

solution.explanation: Changing $100 to $1000 produces a completely different SHA-256 hash (avalanche effect). When Bob verifies, his computed hash won't match the hash recovered from the signature, revealing tampering.

practiceProblems.title: ECDSA Randomness
practiceProblems.description: Why must ECDSA signing use good randomness? What happened when Sony reused random numbers?
practiceProblems.latex: k must be unique per signature
hints: ECDSA signing: s = k^(-1)(h + rd) mod n
If same k used twice: equations relate d

solution.answer: Reusing random number k allows private key recovery from two signatures
solution.explanation: Sony PlayStation 3 used the same k for all signatures. With two signatures (r, s1) and (r, s2) on different messages: k = (h1 - h2) / (s1 - s2). Once k is known, private key d = (sk - h) / r. This completely compromised PS3 security.

snippets.title: RSA Signature with PyCryptodome
snippets.code:
from Crypto.Signature import pkcs1_15
from Crypto.Hash import SHA256
from Crypto.PublicKey import RSA

# Generate key pair
key = RSA.generate(2048)
private_key = key
public_key = key.publickey()

# Message to sign
message = b"Important document to sign"

# Create signature
h = SHA256.new(message)
signer = pkcs1_15.new(private_key)
signature = signer.sign(h)

print(f"Signature: {signature.hex()[:32]}...")
print(f"Signature length: {len(signature)} bytes")

# Verify signature
h = SHA256.new(message)
verifier = pkcs1_15.new(public_key)
try:
    verifier.verify(h, signature)
    print("\nSignature is VALID - message authenticated!")
except (ValueError, TypeError):
    print("\nSignature is INVALID - possible tampering!")

# Try verifying with modified message
modified = b"Important document to sign!"  # Added !
h2 = SHA256.new(modified)
try:
    verifier.verify(h2, signature)
    print("Modified message verified (shouldn't happen)")
except:
    print("Modified message rejected (correct behavior)")

snippets.title: ECDSA Signatures
snippets.code:
from Crypto.PublicKey import ECC
from Crypto.Signature import DSS
from Crypto.Hash import SHA256

# Generate ECC key pair (P-256 curve = equivalent to RSA-3072)
key = ECC.generate(curve='P-256')

print(f"ECC Key size: 256 bits")
print(f"Public key point: ({key.pointQ.x[:16]}..., {key.pointQ.y[:16]}...)")

# Sign message
message = b"Bitcoin-style transaction"
h = SHA256.new(message)
signer = DSS.new(key, mode='fips-186-3')
signature = signer.sign(h)

print(f"\nECDSA Signature: {signature.hex()[:32]}...")
print(f"Signature length: {len(signature)} bytes (shorter than RSA!)")

# Verify
verifier = DSS.new(key.public_key(), mode='fips-186-3')
try:
    verifier.verify(h, signature)
    print("\nECDSA signature VERIFIED!")
except:
    print("\nSignature verification FAILED!")
